title: Testing access control
summary: Prove access control and revocation end to end with canary documents and test principals, red-team the retrieval path against named attack techniques, and keep a leak-response runbook you have rehearsed.
useIf: You operate a RAG system over permissioned content and need evidence that revocation and isolation work.
avoidIf: You only need the mechanism of one ACL option. Use the access control topics first.

explain.md: Test through the **whole stack**: ingest, index, retrieval, cache, prompt, answer and citation. A filter-builder unit test passes while a revoked user still reads a cached answer. The interview probe to practise is: how do you test that revoking access really removes documents from answers? Use a canary document, a revoked test user and an end-to-end check.

explain.caption: A minimum ACL test matrix
head: Case
Setup
Expected
rows: Canary document, user in its group
Same document, user outside the group
Absent from results, citations, caches and logs
Remove the user, wait the stated SLA
User reaches the group through two levels
Present (or absent if the design excludes nesting, as stated)
Delete the canary at the source
Gone from index and caches within the SLA

explain.md: Gate releases on **zero leaks** and watch **recall for restricted callers** as a separate metric, because a safe filter that hides everything also fails. Run the matrix in CI, nightly against production with synthetic principals, and after every ACL, cache or index change. Keep immutable retrieval logs of ids, principal, filter and decision, which OWASP LLM08 recommends [[r2]]. For debugging, use elevated read with a dedicated role rather than the application key [[r12]].

**Red team** the retrieval path with named techniques: indirect injection (AML.T0051.001), RAG poisoning (AML.T0070), gathering RAG-indexed targets (AML.T0064) and exfiltration through agent tool invocation (AML.T0086) [[r4]]. Pair it with detection: Defender for Cloud AI threat protection alerts on data leakage, poisoning and jailbreak attempts for supported Azure AI services, with text tokens only and commercial cloud only [[tr16]].

steps.title: Contain
steps.md: Hide the document or path, purge caches, flip the feature flag.

steps.title: Preserve
steps.md: Freeze retrieval logs: ids, principal, filter, decision.

steps.title: Scope
steps.md: Find who retrieved which documents in the window.

steps.title: Fix
steps.md: Repair the ACL, sync, cache or filter cause and notify as required.

steps.title: Prevent
steps.md: Add the case to the matrix and drill the runbook.

whereToUse: CI and nightly production checks for any permissioned RAG system
Pre-launch security reviews and red-team exercises
Validating that a sync or cache change did not widen access
Incident drills and post-incident regression tests

use: Revocation or isolation is a stated promise
You change ACL sync, caches or the index often
A leak would trigger an incident or a notification duty
avoid: Testing only the filter builder or only the index
Treating a red-team report as a substitute for regression tests
Running tests with an admin identity that bypasses the path users take
flips: Content is public: reduce to a smoke test
Revocation is seconds: test continuously with synthetic principals
A new tool or source appears: add its attack path to the red-team plan

pitfalls.symptom: Tests pass but users report leaks
pitfalls.cause: Tests ran against the index with an admin key, skipping caches and the user token path
pitfalls.fix: Test as a synthetic user through the production path and read results with a normal token

pitfalls.symptom: Revocation test passes in CI and fails in production
pitfalls.cause: Production caches and sync intervals differ from the test setup
pitfalls.fix: Run the canary against production with the real SLA wait

pitfalls.symptom: A fix is deployed and the leak returns next quarter
pitfalls.fix: Every incident adds a case to the matrix

pitfalls.symptom: No one can say who retrieved the leaked document
pitfalls.cause: Retrieval logs hold no principal or document ids
pitfalls.fix: Log ids, principal, filter and decision in an immutable store

scenarios.title: What to test in CI
scenarios.situation: A team has unit tests for the function that builds the filter string and a manual check before release. Last month a revoked user read a cached answer. The team runs a pre-filter plus a semantic cache.
unknowns: Can synthetic users be created in the identity provider?
How long is the cache TTL?
scenarios.question: What do you add first?

options.name: More unit tests for the filter builder
options.why: The leak came from a cache, which the filter builder never touches.
options.tradeoff: Worthwhile as fast feedback beside end-to-end tests.

options.name: An end-to-end canary matrix with allowed, denied, revoked, nested and no-token users, run through the full stack including caches
options.why: It exercises every copy of the permission and would have caught the cached answer.
options.tradeoff: Needs synthetic principals and waiting for the SLA.

options.name: Index-level tests with the admin key
options.why: Checks the ACL data in the index.
options.tradeoff: Skips caches, the token path and the answer.

flips.then: Drop the cache case and keep the revoked-user wait.
Run the canary continuously in production.

scenarios.takeaway: Test every copy of a permission.

scenarios.title: A user shows an HR snippet
scenarios.situation: A user reports that the assistant quoted an HR document they should not see. The assistant serves several thousand users. You have retrieval logs with document ids and principals.
scenarios.question: What do you do in the first hour?

options.name: Investigate the root cause before changing anything
options.why: The document stays exposed while you investigate.
options.tradeoff: Right once containment is in place.

options.name: Contain first: hide the document and purge related caches, then freeze logs, scope who retrieved it, and only then fix the cause
options.why: It stops further exposure and keeps evidence for the scope and notification decision.
options.tradeoff: The document is unavailable to legitimate readers meanwhile.

options.name: Roll back to the previous index version
options.tradeoff: It may restore stale ACLs and drops other legitimate changes.

flips.if: The leak spans a whole scope
flips.then: Disable that source and open a formal incident.
Involve the privacy and legal contacts for notification duties.

scenarios.takeaway: Contain first, then preserve, scope and fix.

scenarios.title: Small red-team budget
scenarios.situation: A team has three days for a red-team exercise on a RAG assistant that reads partner-supplied documents and can call one reply tool. They have a list of 500 generic jailbreak prompts.
unknowns: Which attack paths are already blocked deterministically?
scenarios.question: How do you spend the time?

options.name: Run all 500 generic jailbreak prompts
options.why: They test direct injection and say little about poisoned documents and exits.
options.tradeoff: Useful as a baseline for direct prompt attacks.

options.name: Map the top attack paths to ATLAS techniques, test indirect injection, poisoning and tool exfiltration with real planted documents, and turn findings into regression tests
options.why: It follows how this system can actually be attacked and leaves durable tests [[r4]].
options.tradeoff: Needs a threat model first and fewer total prompts.

options.name: Run an automated scanner and accept its report

flips.if: No tools and no rendering exist

scenarios.takeaway: Red-team the paths your system really has.

quiz.q: Order the first steps of a leak response.
items: Contain: hide the document or path and purge caches
Preserve: freeze retrieval logs with ids, principal and decision
Scope: find who retrieved which documents in the window
Fix the cause and add a regression test
quiz.explain: Containment stops exposure, preserving logs keeps evidence, scoping sizes the impact and the fix plus a regression test prevents a repeat. Investigating before containing leaves the document exposed.

quiz.q: Your ACL tests pass but a revoked user still reads an answer. Which missing test most likely explains it?
options: A unit test for the filter builder
An end-to-end revoked-user test through caches, waiting for the stated SLA
A test of the embedding model's recall
A load test of the search service
quiz.explain: Only an end-to-end revoked-user test through every copy of the permission, including caches, catches a stale answer. Filter-builder, recall and load tests do not exercise revocation.

flashcards.front: What is a canary document test?
flashcards.back: A planted document with known permissions and synthetic users. You check that allowed users get it, denied and revoked users do not, and that deletes propagate, end to end.

flashcards.front: What two metrics gate an ACL release?
flashcards.back: Zero leaks as a hard gate, and recall for restricted callers as a watched metric, since a filter that hides everything also fails.

flashcards.front: Name four ATLAS techniques to red-team a RAG path.
flashcards.back: AML.T0051.001 indirect prompt injection, AML.T0070 RAG poisoning, AML.T0064 gather RAG-indexed targets and AML.T0086 exfiltration via agent tool invocation.
